sections.title: Relating Pressure, Volume, Amount, and Temperature: The Ideal Gas Law
Stoichiometry of Gaseous Substances, Mixtures, and Reactions

variables.meaning: the pressure of a gas, measured on a gauge attached to the vessel that holds it
variables.unit: atm (also kPa, torr, psi and bar, as the measurement is reported)

variables.meaning: the volume of the gas, which is the volume of the vessel that confines it
the amount of gas in the vessel, counted in moles
the temperature of the gas on the kelvin scale, which every gas law calculation requires
the ideal gas constant, also called the universal gas constant, whose value follows from the units the pressure, volume and temperature are written in
variables.unit: 0.08206 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, or 8.314 kPa L mol⁻¹ K⁻¹

variables.meaning: the pressure of a confined gas in its first condition, before the change the problem describes
the pressure of the same gas in its second condition, after the change
the volume of a confined gas in its first condition
the volume of the same gas in its second condition
the kelvin temperature of a confined gas in its first condition
the kelvin temperature of the same gas in its second condition
the amount of a confined gas in its first condition, counted in moles
the amount of the same gas in its second condition

equations.condition: a fixed amount of gas held at constant volume, with both temperatures on the kelvin scale
a fixed amount of gas held at constant pressure, with both temperatures on the kelvin scale
a fixed amount of gas held at constant temperature
a confined gas held at constant pressure and constant temperature
a gas behaving ideally, which is a good approximation at relatively low pressures and high temperatures
a fixed amount of an ideal gas under two different sets of conditions

glossary.definition: temperature at which the volume of a gas would be zero according to Charles’s law.
(also, Gay-Lussac’s law) pressure of a given number of moles of gas is directly proportional to its kelvin temperature when the volume is held constant
volume of a gas at constant temperature and pressure is proportional to the number of gas molecules
volume of a given number of moles of gas held at constant temperature is inversely proportional to the pressure under which it is measured
volume of a given number of moles of gas is directly proportional to its kelvin temperature when the pressure is held constant
hypothetical gas whose physical properties are perfectly described by the gas laws
constant derived from the ideal gas equation R = 0.08206 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ or 8.314 L kPa mol⁻¹ K⁻¹
relation between the pressure, volume, amount, and temperature of a gas under conditions derived by combination of the simple gas laws

glossary.term: standard conditions of temperature and pressure (STP)

glossary.definition: volume of 1 mole of gas at STP, approximately 22.4 L for gases behaving ideally
